metadata.title: Good News Club v. Milford Central School, 533 U.S. 98 (2001) (No. 99-2036)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Good News Club v. Milford Central School

Opinion filed: 2001-06-11

Docket No.: 99-2036

Citations:
• 150 L. Ed. 2d 151
• 121 S. Ct. 2093
• 533 U.S. 98
• 2001 U.S. LEXIS 4312

Case holding summaries:
• "‘[T]he reasonable observer in the endorsement inquiry must be deemed aware of the history and context of the community and forum in which the religious [speech takes place]’"
• emphasizing that Estab- lishment Clause does not create a "heckler’s veto"
• holding that Establishment Clause did not require public school to bar evangelical Christian student group from using facilities accessed by various other groups
• holding that "speech discussing otherwise permissible subjects cannot be excluded from a .. . forum on the ground that the subject is discussed from a religious viewpoint"
• stating that "no one disputes that the Club instructs children to overcome feelings of jealousy, to treat others well, . . . and to be obedient, even if it does so in a nonsecular way"
• applying the reasonable and viewpoint neutral test to a limited public forum
• identifying limited public fora as subject to the same test as nonpublic fora described in, for example, Lamb's Chapel v. Ctr. Moriches Union Free Sch. Dist., 508 U.S. 384, 392, 113 S.Ct. 2141, 124 L.Ed.2d 352 (1993)
• “Because allowing the Club to speak on 12 school grounds would ensure neutrality, not threaten it, [the 13 school district] faces an uphill battle in arguing that the 14 Establishment Clause compels it to exclude the Good News Club.”
• noting that the State's restrictions on speech are subject to stricter scrutiny in traditional or open public forums, than are restrictions in a limited public forum
• holding that denying access to school facilities to Bible club that sought to teach "morals and character" from an evangelical religious perspective was viewpoint discrimination
• holding that a school violated the First Amendment when it prohibited (5th Cir. 1966
• invalidating school’s restriction on an outside religious group’s use of a school’s multipurpose facility after school hours
• noting that “it is not clear whether a State’s interest in avoiding an Establishment Clause violation would justify viewpoint discrimination.”
• "The State may be justified `in reserving [its forum] for certain groups or for the discussion of certain topics.'" (quoting Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of Univ. of Va., 515 U.S. 819, 829, 115 S.Ct. 2510, 132 L.Ed.2d 700 (1995)
• "The State may be justified `in reserving [its forum] for certain groups or for the discussion of certain topics.'" (quoting Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of Univ. of Va., 515 U.S. 819, 829, 115 S.Ct. 2510, 132 L.Ed.2d 700 (1995)) (alteration in original)
• excluding religious club from meeting after hours at school is unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination
• “[W]e conclude[ ] that attendance at the graduation exercise was obligatory.”
• "We decline to employ Establishment Clause jurisprudence using a modified heckler's veto...."
• applying the First Amendment Free Speech Clause to students "ages 6 to 12"
• discussing the difference between subject matter regulations and viewpoint discrimination
• applying forum analysis where private speech occurs on government property
• "We have said that a state interest in avoiding an Establishment Clause violation `may be characterized as compelling,' and therefore may justify content-based discrimination."
• finding that activities "quintessentially religious" in nature such as religious instruction, prayer, and discussion and recitation of the Bible, are protected speech
• "[A] significant factor in upholding governmental programs in the face of Establishment Clause attack is their neutrality towards religion"
• weighing the validity of a school's Establishment Clause defense after finding that the challenged restriction constituted viewpoint discrimination and that strict scrutiny therefore applied
• holding that Establishment Clause did not require public school to bar evangelical Christian student group from using facilities accessed by various other groups
• stating that reasonable observer would know about non- neutral implementation of policy
• public schools cannot deny after-school use of facilities to religious programs
• applying the First Amendment Free Speech Clause to students “ages 6 to 12”
• "[obviously when individuals who are not schoolteachers are giving lessons after school to children permitted to attend only with parental consent, the concerns expressed in Edwards are not present."
• treating as limited public forum school district's opening of school facilities for after-hours assembly of private organizations
• noting that the prohibited actions were “religious instruction and Bible study”
• "When the State established a limited public forum, the State is not required to and does not allow persons to engage in every type of speech. The State may be justified in reserving its forum for certain groups or for the discussion of certain topics."
• rejecting subjective, speculative listeners' perception argument as "a modified heckler's veto, in which a group's religious activity can be proscribed on the basis of what the youngest members of the audience might misperceive"
• use of school facilities by community groups
• finding that activities "quintessentially religious" in nature such as religious instruction, prayer, and discussion and recitation of the Bible, are protected speech
• holding that school could not exclude from use of its facilities a Christian club for children when it had made its facilities a limited public forum for afterschool activities
• not applying the Lemon test
• holding that allowing religious school groups to use school facilities does not violate the Establishment Clause
• "[T]o the extent we consider whether the community would feel coercive pressure to engage in the Club's activities, the relevant community would be the parents, not the elementary school children."
• invalidating school’s restriction on an outside religious group’s use of a school’s multipurpose facility after school hours
• noting that “it is not clear whether a State’s interest in avoiding an Establishment Clause violation would justify viewpoint discrimination.”
• holding that a school violated the First Amendment when it prohibited a private Christian organization for children aged six to twelve from holding meetings at the school for the purpose of singing Christian songs, hearing Bible lessons, and memorizing scripture
• use of Nor do the materials at issue here school facilities by community groups
• holding that a school's exclusion of Christian children's club from meeting after hours at school based on its religious nature was unconstitutional
• "[W]e have held that a significant factor in upholding governmental programs in the face of Establishment Clause attack is their neutrality towards religion."
• holding 13 that, according its “Community Use Policy” establishing the limited 14 forum, “there is no question that teaching morals and character 15 development to children is a permissible purpose under Milford’s 16 policy”
• finding few 1 religious groups whose presence would convey to the public the 2 message that the government endorses religion (or a particular 3 religion
• “[W]hen the subject 19 matter is morals and character, it is quixotic to attempt a 20 distinction between religious viewpoints and religious subject 21 matters.”
• invalidating school’s restriction on an outside religious group’s use of a school’s multipurpose facility after school hours
